speechtext:
The situation we are discussing tonight can be found all across Canada. Last week calves in my part of the country were given away because they had no value. They are not killing calves in Alberta, but they are of little worth. It is unfortunate that the situation in Quebec was dramatized the way it was, but we must recognize that it happened and that we have to live with it. I consider it immoral to destroy food in a world where there are hungry people.
Let me return to the lack of government policy. One of the first bills that the minister presented to the House of Commons was a crop insurance bill. We wanted to amend that bill but the minister would not accept our amendment. If he had accepted the amendment, it would have encouraged' farmers not to go into the cattle business but remain in the production of grain. They tried to use the cattle industry as a buffer, so that if one aspect of agriculture failed they would be protected to some extent.
The minister in charge of the Wheat Board (Mr. Lang) has promised to bring in a stabilization program. If this program works it will be to the benefit of the agricultural industry, but it will run counter to the crop insurance program introduced by the Minister of Agriculture. There is not room for both, but if the crop insurance program were made to work properly, it would stabilize the grain industry to a great degree and there would be no need of a grain stabilization program.
I am sorry that people are suffering as they are at the present time, but the Minister of Agriculture will not accept any advice offered from this side of the House. We have made suggestions which he did not accept. When he introduced the present beef subsidy program I said at the time it would be of no benefit to the producer unless chaos hit the industry, and I say the same thing today.
The hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) dealt in detail with the minister's beef subsidy program, which is based on a 45.42 cents a pound average over the year. If the cost of putting on a pound of beef is 60 cents, this subsidy is 15 cents below the cost of production. The fellow in the beef feeding industry will try to protect himself, so he in turn is going to buy that animal at 15 cents below the subsidy price, which means that the selling price of the animal is down around 30 cents a pound. There is no way the cow-calf operator, in these days of inflation, can exist receiving 30 cents a pound for his calves, but there is a chance that he could survive with 40 cents a pound.
It is rather ironic, Madam Speaker, that a year ago last spring fat cattle were being sold in Alberta for 42 cents a pound, or $42 a hundredweight. At 42 cents a pound the beef producers had never made more money in their lives out of the cattle industry. This year, 12 months later, they were selling their cattle at 45 cents to 48 cents a pound, and they have never seen a time in history when they were losing money faster. The reason is, of course, the inflation factor which has hit the industry and the cost of production, something the government has failed to consider or to deal with adequately; hence the problem at the present time.

I sincerely hope the government does not try to ride out this dilemma on the backs of the grain producers. I am sure the Minister of Agriculture will agree with me when I say that the grain producer is finally getting a price for his product that will enable him to survive and to buy a few of the things he has been waiting for for so long.
The grain producer has gone through a very difficult period in the last several years and I sincerely hope the government does not adopt a policy that is disadvantageous to him in order to offset or circumvent another serious situation, in this case the dilemma we are debating tonight. The minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board has been hesitant about establishing an initial price within an acceptable ratio.
Today No. 1 barley is worth $3 on the world market yet the western grain grower is receiving $1.35. That does not make sense unless the government is trying to manipulate the producer into a position where he will have to sell his grain for feed, thereby getting the government off the hook. I hope it is not too long before the minister establishes an initial price for grain that will convince the producer he is not being used to get the government off the hook in so far as the livestock industry is concerned.
I remember the Minister of Agriculture standing up in this House telling the agricultural people to produce to beat the band. That is what they did, and now what has happened? Some 28 million eggs have gone bad, and we have a cattle situation he does not know how to correct. Until the government comes up with a long range agricultural policy for the benefit of the people, we will get nowhere. The government will continue to jump from crisis to crisis, and no matter how hopping mad the Minister of Agriculture gets, as he did tonight, we will get nowhere.
I hope the government sits down and establishes a long range agricultural policy for the benefit of the producer and the consumer, without manipulating one segment of the industry against the other. Canada needs a policy today which will afford the producer a certain degree of protection, guaranteeing that he will not be producing at a loss. If the time comes when we have a general shortage the person who will suffer most is the consumer. After all the agricultural industry is engaged in producing something for the consumer, and if that industry does not produce we will be in a sorry situation in a world which is becoming hungrier and hungrier as the days go by.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   AGRICULTURE DESTRUCTION OF CALVES AND HIGH RETAIL PRICE OF MEAT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, who knows what tomorrow holds? One week, we hear that millions of eggs are being destroyed, the other week that wheat was spoiled in the west last winter, then we hear of problems concerning milk, whole milk, powdered milk, industrial milk. Then we hear that there are not enough workers to harvest fruits and vegetables, and this happens all across Canada. Tonight, after listening to half a dozen liberal members, I find that not one of them has suggested a solution to the problem, not even the minister. We ponder over the facts, and we say to ourselves: we are going to look for a solution, but we always wait until the
October 31, 1974

situation is a real mess before we start to discuss solutions.
Madam Speaker, I ask: who knows what tomorrow holds? That is especially true of this situation. Four months ago, we had a federal election. The liberals are on the treasury benches. That is true. At that time, a dozen ministers visited the Saguenay-Lake St. John area. The Prime Minister flew there by helicopter. The member for Lake St. John (Mr. Lessard) was there and at that time the liberal party had all the money they needed to buy the "two-footed calves" of the area. At that time, they did have the money. Four months later, the same party is in power and it no longer has enough money to buy fourfooted calves.
That is a paradox, Madam Speaker. Last night, on television, I watched calves being slaughtered. The member for Lake St. John says the calves were not slaughtered. No, they were doing the same thing as in slaughter-houses. The only thing is that in slaughter-houses, this is done behind closed doors. Last night it was done in public. And this is not a slaughter! What makes it a slaughter is not that they killed the calves. We know that when calves are sent to the slaughter-house, only the bones are taken away, and the meat goes to the consumers.
In Saint-Bruno, the meat went into the hole, along with the bones. The calves were buried with milk, eggs and some dirt. It did happen in the Lac Saint-Jean area. It is unthinkable! It reminds me of what happened 40 years ago. That was a long time ago. In 1934, wheat was burnt in western Canada, because the crisis was international. The next day potatoes were burnt or dipped in washing-blue in New Brunswick, because there were too many potatoes. Thousands of bags of flour were thrown in lake Superior, lake Erie and lake Ontario, because there was a world crisis.
Meanwhile there were unemployed in Canada. Families were not even getting welfare allowances because they did not exist then. A massive destruction of farm and other products took place. The same situation is happening all over again, but we are told: No, there will not be an economic crisis. Was not the destruction of animals in Saint-Bruno an insult to our poor and needy families? Nothing is said about those families. We talk about surpasses in Europe. Production of meat, wheat and other products has begun. Since we are no longer able to export, then let us quietly poop out here. What does that mean? Instead of finding a system that would allow the Canadian consumer to dig into his immense resources, we are being lulled by those words: Sorry, but there was nothing else the farmers could do.
Madam Speaker, the situation is serious and not only in agriculture but no solution is put forward in that field nor in any other field.
I asked the minister a question not long ago. Well, he said, the beef industry is the concern of the Quebec Minister of Agriculture. Quebec says: Marketing comes under Ottawa. We are witnessing a poker game. The buck is passed from the province of Quebec to the federal government and nothing is settled. Attempts are made to lull the people to sleep, but they will not be easily fooled.
Slaughter of Calves
Twenty-five years ago, when I was a backbencher, I said, as I say again today, that farming, the farm, the farmers, are the very foundation of the whole economic and social structure of Canada. Dress coats and beaver hats would turn to dust if it were not for the farmers, and yet we wait! The hon. member for Lapointe (Mr. Marceau) finds that amusing. But it is true! Everyone knows it.
The farmer is praised, but he is not given the means to live decently. His is the social class that is most neglected by the governments of Quebec and Ottawa. All other groups of society have obtained working conditions the farmers have been denied. The farmer is "trapped" at home, seven days a week, without holidays, summer or winter. He has to milk the cows, morning and night: they never go on strike. The farmer is tied down to his job. Our attention turns to him only when we are up against such situations as this one. Otherwise, we take no notice. No one offers solutions. What is the solution?
Twenty-five years ago, I suggested building refrigerated warehouses and others in which to store food produce when it cannot be sold; those stocks would eventually be sold normally. The government should give financial assistance to that type of construction, as it did, up to a point, for the storage of wheat. It was not done in the case of meat. That is left up to the big companies.
A while ago, the hon. member for Kamloops-Cariboo (Mr. Marchand) said there may be too many middlemen between the farmer and the consumer. It may be true, but what is the government waiting for? Why does it not help the farmers to set up public markets where the consumer could buy directly from the farmer? That would do away with the thieves between the two. Though I must say some distributors are honest.
We have seen backers of electoral party funds, like the fellow Obront, in Montreal, who got caught up to his neck by the underworld for having financed the provincial liberal party. Madam Speaker, those are the people who devour both consumer and producer, the producer who now sells his veal 15 cents a pound in Quebec, when it costs him 43 cents a pound to feed the calf.
As mentioned a while ago, in Saskatchewan beef was paid 8 cents a pound. How come store prices do not change? The other day, last Friday, I bought four T-bone steaks and paid $12 for them; that is the price of a calf at Saint-Bruno.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   AGRICULTURE DESTRUCTION OF CALVES AND HIGH RETAIL PRICE OF MEAT
speechtext: They are not yet on the market, the calves of Saint-Bruno.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   AGRICULTURE DESTRUCTION OF CALVES AND HIGH RETAIL PRICE OF MEAT
speechtext:
They are not yet on the market. Madam Speaker, this is terrible.
In the Ottawa area, a committee investigates supermarkets, A.L. Raymond, IGA, Steinberg and others, to compare prices. We hear on television that A.L. Raymond has much lower prices than the others. After having examined the reports, we note that they are on the bottom of the list and that they have the highest prices. The reports were useful for adjusting prices a little. Whether it is A.L. Raymond or another, I don't care. But it was good for adjusting prices a little. It established competition. There should be such committees in all Canadian cities to make comparisons between stores and to tell the consumer who

October 31, 1974
Slaughter of Calves
is selling at the best price. It is a way of curbing inflation. It is not only a question of noting, inventing or seeking, but of obtaining adequate prices. One sells at a higher price than the other, they say. If the public is informed about it, we will witness a price readjustment.
In the meantime, as far as agriculture is concerned, the only solution is to subsidize farmers, allowing them to make a profit on their cattle, to store meat for consumption when it cannot be sold, either through cooperatives, or by building storage facilities, or by establishing agricultural markets where the consumer will be able to buy at a decent price while bearing in mind that some profit must be paid to the producer.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   AGRICULTURE DESTRUCTION OF CALVES AND HIGH RETAIL PRICE OF MEAT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me to talk on a subject which, I am sure, leaves all the hon. members embarrassed. I think that no member in this House is very happy tonight, after having seen yesterday evening the television program on the demonstration of the Alma union group, especially when, at the end of the program, we were told that people starve in Bangladesh or India, for example. In Canada and particularly in the province of Quebec, we want to express our dissatisfaction with an agricultural situation by slaughtering calves.
It is not for me to judge such a situation. I do not think that farmers are involved because they love their animals. If they have reached that point, it is because they want us to hear their cry of anguish.
I shall endeavour, Madam Speaker, to make a brief review and then offer some solutions to the present problem. It is a most complex one. Agriculture cannot be compared to the shoe industry. Several factors limit our farmers' income, and I shall only list a few and devell a little more on the two main factors that have brought about this situation. Among the factors that could limit the producers' income when it involves a plant production, let us say that those producers are always under tension or subject to factors which could definitely restrict their crops, namely insects or weather. There is also the fact that these products are perishable. It is sometimes difficult to bring them to the market when prices are more or less attractive. We are dealing with products with short or long production cycles. And yet we cannot turn on the tap when we need some product and turn it off three months later when we say that the consumer market can no longer absorb those products. It is still an other element that may limit the economic aspect of the agricultural industry. A regular supply must be provided. Our economists tell us that an increase of more than 4 per cent of consumption is enough to lower prices much below the production costs.
And now my last point: there is no relation between the finished product's production costs and the sales price's production costs, between the production costs and the sales price. This is precisely the problem facing us tonight, that is the gap between the sales price and the production costs. Since there is no relation between the two, the producer who had to process grain finds himself in this situation which we could express in figures. I have here the report published by Statistics Canada, Agriculture Division, on a comparison of receipts from farm products. From January to August 1974, the overall amount is $3,190 million compared with $824 million for 1970. I am referring

to crops like wheat, oat, barley. With regard to cattle and other similar products, for the same period, we note for 1974 an amount of $2,725 million and for 1970, of $1,700 million. So we note an increase more than fourfold compared with the 1970 figures. But relating to cattle, we have barely a one billion dollars increase. This shows to what extent there is no relation between the gross product and the finished product's sales price.
Madam Speaker, I think that with regard to our Canadian agricultural industry, the objectives of the Department of Agriculture are as follows: we want to develop an agricultural industry that is stong, dynamic and competitive on all international markets. I feel that on this point we have succeeded because Canadian farmers are among the most knowledgeable in the world. We come first both in terms of quality and productivity as far as farm products are concerned.
Canadian farmers have bred the best Holsteins. They have developed the best wheat, the best layers, the best beef, the best dairy products, and so on and so forth. Canadian farmers are responsible for the best products in the world.
We have achieved our first aim. This productivity has not always been to the advantage of producers. When we consider the percentage of the family budget earmarked for food, we realize that consumers in Canada, compared with those in other countries, have largely benefited from this increased productivity by farm producers. In Canada, today, the percentage of the budget earmarked for food can be favourably compared with Italy, where one-third of the budget is used to buy food. In Great Britain, Sweden and Canada, these percentages are 25, 25 and 19 per cent respectively. This means that the first objective of the Department of Agriculture has certainly been reached.
As a second objective, we should see to it that Canadian farmers get higher incomes, in line at least with those received by workers in others sectors of our economy. This is a subject which we should pounder more. In fact, we have already done so.
We have won the Productivity Cup, a trophy which testifies to the quality of our products. Here is an example: Although our cars may be powered by very powerful engines, if we do not improve our roads, accidents may occur. In the area of farm products, if we increase production without regard for the needs of consumers, accidents may also occur. Legislation and standards dealing with production are essential. Well, this is exactly what we have done and we wish to continue to regulate this production.
A moment ago, I heard the hon. member for Saint-Hya-cinthe (Mr. Wagner) argue that it is necessary, for justice's sake, to go all out and to strain our budget to the limit.
I think that production should be set to order as there is a marketing and distribution problem. This is precisely what we have been trying to do.
One remembers that when we established national marketing boards, we tried for two years in this House to put some order in production, while the members opposite

were condemning everyone of our efforts. The Progressive Conservative Party has systematically objected to the creation of marketing boards, but a Canadian association of beef producers demonstrated their support for such a national marketing board with a view to regulating production in cooperation with consumer markets.
The Progressive Conservative members have objected to the creation of a marketing mechanism to ensure a return to producers for their investments.
I think if we consider the dairy industry, we will find that producers cover their costs, and the increase in production costs has affected that industry as well. Nevertheless, they cover their costs and there is a national marketing board which is the Canadian Dairy Commission. There is also another marketing agency called the Canadian Wheat Board.
Madam Speaker, I would like to mention about this marketing problem and the increase in production costs that since there is a marketing agency, that is the Canadian Wheat Board, we should, according to the wish of the Farmers' Union, have some representation in this agency. Going back to the year 68, 69, and 70, when the world price of wheat was lower than the domestic price, producers and consumers from eastern Canada have agreed to pay a premium in order to secure at least a normal income to western grain producers. But it seems to me that the principle acknowledged through the establishment of the Farm Products Marketing Board was a worthwhile one, providing for a distribution of members in agencies and in the Council. Well now, we also have consumers at the agencies level. I suggest that we should have at least one consumer representative from the eastern provinces within the Canadian Wheat Board.
Therefore, I would ask for a review of the Canadian Wheat Board powers, so that eastern producers who consume 75 per cent of the food grain produced in Canada, may benefit from it. I would also consider as a normal step, if we have acknowledged the principle whereby consumers should be represented within the Canadian Marketing Board, that the Eastern provinces should also be represented on the Canadian Wheat Board.
In conclusion, Madam Speaker, I say that the success of the farming industry depends not only on the farmer himself and his suppliers but also on those at the various marketing steps. Then, we should appeal to the goodwill of everyone directly related to the problem of foodstuffs marketing.
I fully agree with the hon. member who a little while ago has expressed the view that our producers do want to produce. There is no doubt, about that and this is not really a matter of production. We are sure that there is no problem at the production level. It is rather the marketing and the distribution aspects that cause some difficulties and I think that the mechanism capable of putting some order into farm production is precisely the marketing boards system.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   AGRICULTURE DESTRUCTION OF CALVES AND HIGH RETAIL PRICE OF MEAT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this is a really strange world. Every one of my
Slaughter of Calves
colleagues who has risen in the House tonight has said that he was pleased to take part in this debate which is dealing with a very serious crisis. This crisis is affecting not only Canadians but people throughout the world. I suppose that farmers will learn something from this debate, if no one else does.
I suppose that the farmers have learned something from the many acts that have been committed in Canada recently, acts which other groups of people have committed to gain the attention of parliament. I suppose that farmers have felt that by orchestrating a slaughter or a massacre-as some of my colleagues have termed it-they could gain the attention of parliament. So, finally, they have gained attention, but it is the attention of the government they have gained, not that of parliament. There were all kinds of people in parliament in the last week or so who have brought to the attention of the government the fact that there is a serious crisis in the lumber industry, and in the food industry, but it took a token act of that nature to get this matter debated in the House.
I am a practical man and I wonder what happened to the romance of being a western rancher that people in the east of Canada, and people in other countries, have dreamt about. I will not speak about the causes of this crisis in which we find ourselves. The purpose of this debate should have been to find a solution-the cause is not important now that we have gone this far. Farmers have lost confidence, they are helpless, and this is why they are massacring calves.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has not offered any solution tonight. He could not complete his speech, and I was tempted to rise and plead with Mr. Speaker to please extend the minister's time so that he would come up with some solution. However, the rule did not permit the minister more time to complete his remarks. Perhaps it is for that reason that he could not give us a solution to the problem. He also is a practical man, and I half expected him to say that perhaps we should invent a birth control pill for cows.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   AGRICULTURE DESTRUCTION OF CALVES AND HIGH RETAIL PRICE OF MEAT
speechtext: Or abortion.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   AGRICULTURE DESTRUCTION OF CALVES AND HIGH RETAIL PRICE OF MEAT
speechtext:
Yes, or something like that.
The causes of all this are the anti-inflation policy in the United States, the policy in Canada to stabilize the grain industry, and certainly the forecasting by the people responsible for that work. The minister said in his speech that there was a global over-supply of beef. If we speak about the basic principles of economics, there is not a sufficient demand for beef in the world.
Several of my colleagues have said the same thing, that there is an over supply and an under-demand for beef. My God, there has never been a time in the history of this world when there was a greater demand for food, including beef. However, there is no demand for beef with the price tag that we put on it. Not only is there not enough demand within Canada for beef at that price, because there are some people in our society who cannot afford that price tag, but there is certainly a shortage of people in this world who can afford the price that we have put on our agricultural products, not only we in Canada but other major agricultural producing countries as well.

October 31, 1974
Slaughter of Calves
I am sorry that I have to say this here, but I cannot help but put myself in the position of a young, growing child in Bangladesh. It is not very hard for me to do that because I have been in such a position, I have experienced it. I daresay that there are not very many people sitting here tonight who can say the same.
This young boy in Bangladesh sees death around him every day. He watches his immediate family die. He watches his mother leave the place where they eat every day without touching the food because she wants to reserve every last particle that is available for her children. I cannot help but fear that perhaps the small boy, in this modern world of communications today, by some strange accident will read some of the press reports that have appeared in our newspapers in Canada lately. One reporter described the scene of horror in Quebec in this way:
The tiny black and white calf stumbled in a struggle to escape and its tiny hoofs slid in the blood soaking the scaffold hanging over a 30-foot-deep pit.
Roughly hauled to its feet, it grew calm, or at least motionless, as its brown eyes stared at the hundreds of carcasses below.
I could go on reading this, but my time is limited. However, it is a beautiful story. I am looking at this small boy who, by sheer accident, reads something like this, and at the same time he might be looking at the eyes of a person dying of starvation. I wonder if anybody here has ever looked into the eyes of a dying person. I have. You can see the sign in the eyes of a dying person for the whole day before his death. It is a terrible story to tell here and I know it shocks people, but obviously it is the only way in which to gain the attention of people. There are people starving to death in the world every day. There are headlines in any of the newspapers at which you would like to look. One of the articles reads as follows:
There is a severe famine throughout the country, and the most conservative estimates say 750,000 persons will likely die of starvation or diseases related to malnutrition from August through November this year.
We are living in a global community; we are talking about our immigration laws and about our responsibility to open up our borders to people from other countries, and yet we allow people in other countries to starve to death while we dump our foodstuffs.
Another thing that I have experienced, that the little boy in Bangladesh might also experience, is to have lived in a country where people were starving to death and, at the time, to have read that North America was dumping wheat into the ocean, dumping flour into the sea to maintain some kind of market stability. The press is full of stories about our rotten eggs. The global community which has access to radio and television will hear and read about those rotten eggs in Canada, about the calves we are slaughtering, and about the wheat we are dumping into the sea. I am very concerned about what this small boy might be thinking and I have an idea what it is, but I will not spatter the pages of Hansard with it. I will tell you one thing he will be thinking. If he ever gets the chance, and he likely never will, there will be an equalization of the score. However, we do not have to worry about that because he likely will never have the chance.

We have an oversupply of expensive beef and an overdemand for inexpensive beef. We must find a balance. We must consider the consequences of a great number of these small boys who say that some day they will have to equal the score. The consequences must eventually be a total collapse of our system, and even a global war as people in other countries watch us waste, destroy and commit criminal acts as we have done. I consider it to be almost a criminal act to discourage farmers and others from producing all the food they can. The solution must obviously be for them to produce all they can.
We cannot pass laws to restrict Canadian farmers from producing the maximum. We must look at who has the responsibility of paying the bill. Certainly everyone is entitled to a profit. Everyone is entitled at least to break even. However, it has been amply demonstrated this evening that the farmer has not been breaking even. The marketer and the processor have not done too badly.
The farmer is entitled to a profit even though he is dealing in food that is hard to come by for consumers. He can be compared with the person who drives an ambulance. Because some poor guy is lying in the ditch bleeding to death it does not mean the ambulance driver should not receive any pay. He is entitled to make a living.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   AGRICULTURE DESTRUCTION OF CALVES AND HIGH RETAIL PRICE OF MEAT
speechtext: The good Samaritan did that.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   AGRICULTURE DESTRUCTION OF CALVES AND HIGH RETAIL PRICE OF MEAT
speechtext: The farmers have been good Samaritans. They have played their role. There are more consumers in this country than farmers. The government should take the side of the farmer and equalize the responsibility. If it is fair for the farmer just to break even, it must be fair for the processor and the consumer just to break even. If it is fair just to break even, then anyone who receives a day's pay is responsible for the situation. If we look at it in that way, it is not hard to find a solution. We have to pay the farmer to keep these calves alive and feed them through the winter. We might even have to pay him to put them out to pasture next year and feed them next fall.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   AGRICULTURE DESTRUCTION OF CALVES AND HIGH RETAIL PRICE OF MEAT
speechtext: But he doesn't want us to interfere.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   AGRICULTURE DESTRUCTION OF CALVES AND HIGH RETAIL PRICE OF MEAT
speechtext:
What I am talking about obviously does not fit into the hon. member's philosophy. I do not think there is much common ground. I am saying we must allow the farmer to break even. It is a responsibility we must all face, whether we are electricians, storekeepers or whatever. Because it is a problem of society, it is something the government must face.
The government must make it possible for the farmer to make it through the winter. He should be given an advance for each calf born last spring or during the summer. He could be given an advance of $100 a head, interest free. This could be repaid after the eventual sale of the calf.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   AGRICULTURE DESTRUCTION OF CALVES AND HIGH RETAIL PRICE OF MEAT
speechtext: Like Saskatchewan did.

speechtext:
Saskatchewan implemented something like that, as did Alberta and other provinces. The federal government must enter into partnership with the provinces. If that is what it takes to overcome this situation, that is what we have to do.
October 31, 1974

This debate should have been designed to find a solution. We should put a dollar figure on what is necessary. I am a small rancher and, therefore, probably one of the reasons for this problem. I am a gentleman farmer. I consider ranching to be a romantic game. I have never really had to work at it, and walk through those brown things scattered all over the field. I see my time is up, Madam Speaker.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   AGRICULTURE DESTRUCTION OF CALVES AND HIGH RETAIL PRICE OF MEAT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I do not often find myself making speeches at this hour of the night. However, I am glad to do so because this is an extremely important subject. I want to speak about an aspect I think is of very great importance. Although the resolution before us does not explicitly refer to the international crisis, that crisis exists. It is clearly related to what we are discussing here.
We are discussing the destruction of food in the context of the world food conference at Rome which starts next week. That destruction of food has implications not only for Canada but the world.
The situation that faces the world has been set out very clearly in the material prepared for the world food conference. I do not have time to go into it in detail, but it is estimated by experts that roughly 460 million people are in a state of chronic malnutrition, with all that that means for the energy, vitality, lives and even the mental development as well as the physical development of those people.
In addition to that chronic situation there is the problem of the starvation emergency that is facing the world. There are estimates by genuine experts, not scaremongers, that there is a prospect of between 25 and 75 million people dying of starvation within a very few months. Therefore, we face a human problem, a problem of human suffering.
In this context the destruction of food raises moral issues. I am not going to suggest we should point the finger at the producers because of the incidents here that precipitated this debate. I am quite sure the people involved would not have dreamed of doing what they did unless they felt obliged to call attention to the fact that the system we have is not providing them with the incentive or, indeed, the means to produce food in a needy world.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) will be one of Canada's spokesmen at this conference in Rome. At least that is the last I heard. I do not know whether he has changed his mind. In any event, I hope he will be there. I will say something about his presence there later. What I want to say is that this conference will give Canada an opportunity for practical leadership. Canada will be looking to the minister and his Cabinet colleagues to give that practical leadership at the conference in Rome.
One of the things we must do is to maximize food production not only in Canada, not only in the west, but throughout the world. It is true that a major responsibility rests with the developing nations to increase their own production and look after their own needs. But international action is needed to make this possible. They need capital and other forms of assistance which it is possible for us to supply.
Slaughter of Calves
It is also my belief that fundamental changes in the marketing system are required, not only in Canada but in other countries. It must be recognized that the agricultural industry or, to make it more personal, the farmers, are entitled to stable prices. They are entitled to economic security to the same extent as anybody else in the community, perhaps more. For that purpose, in our view, national marketing boards and other marketing boards are required. But there is also need for international action which would stabilize world prices for both producers and consumers throughout the world.
One proposal which I hope the minister and his colleagues will be putting forward in Rome concerns the establishment of an effective world food price reserve, or world food price bank to provide the security which is required, and prevent the boom and bust cycle which is beneficial neither to consumers or producers. I believe we should work for fundamental social changes. They are imperative. Although we are speaking of crises there is one advantage about them-they give rise to times of decision. We are now at a stage when the world food crisis requires decisions to be made.
I shall not attempt to run over all the suggestions which have been made to deal with the situation. What is needed is a comprehensive and flexible world food policy, making provision not only for wider research but a co-ordinated national stock policy embodied in international undertakings.
I shall conclude a few minutes before the allotted time but, before I do so, I would say this to the Minister of Agriculture: I hope he will approach the conference in Rome in a slightly different spirit from that in which he approached this debate. I hope he will listen with humility to what is said by those who represent other nations at that conference.
In particular, I believe we have a lot to learn from the so-called Third World, whose people are most endangered by the food prices we are discussing. I hope the minister will come forward at that conference with specific, practical proposals, which will call for continuity after the conference has ended so that the conference will not be solely an occasion for rhetoric, procedural debate and a few pious resolutions, but the beginning of co-ordinated, international action to deal with the gravest problems facing the planet, that is, the task of providing food for all the men, women and children in the world.

maintopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 26   AGRICULTURE DESTRUCTION OF CALVES AND HIGH RETAIL PRICE OF MEAT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) talked tonight about confusion. There is a lot of confusion in this House tonight. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) talked about the beef industry in general. The hon. member for Prince George-Peace River (Mr. Oberle), when he wasn't waffling about Bangladesh, also talked about the beef industry.
The problem is not the beef industry in Canada. The problem is the cow-calf operation. Let me illustrate this by giving some data. Slaughter cattle prices in Calgary have gone from $46.50 for Al, A2 steers in 1973 to $48.25 a hundredweight in 1974. That is an increase of $1.75 a hundredweight. The story is similar in the case of A3 and A4 steers. It is only in the case of commercial steers that

October 31, 1974
Slaughter of Calves
the price has gone down $1.50 from $40.50 a hundredweight in 1973 to $39 a hundredweight in 1974. The big decline in price relates specifically to cows. In the week ending October 19, 1973, D1 and D2 live cows were selling for $36.75, and in 1974 the price was $21.
It is recognized that cow-calf farmers are experiencing a problem and we must work positively and constructively to resolve it, and do so quickly.
The Ontario Federation of Agriculture has recommended to the Ontario government that a program be launched which would enable beef farmers to keep their herds intact, rather that force them to slaughter cattle because they cannot afford to feed them. This program would involve payments of $100 for each culled cow slaughtered for sale, and $25 for each calf introduced into or maintained in a herd. In the short term, this would provide cash to the farmer to improve his cash flow problem. In the long term, this would provide safeguards against a possible future situation in which we might be faced with a shortage of beef, perhaps as soon as 1976. Such a shortage may develop if farmers continue to slaughter feeder calves.
In order to maintain herds in the best condition, and still allow for some thinning out in order to save feed costs, it is suggested that a certain percentage of a herd, say 20 per cent of the poorest quality cattle, be slaughtered. These could be sold as cutters and canners, and the breeding stock would not be depleted as is now the case.
This would improve the quality of the herds and contribute to improving agricultural efficiency, as well as answer the criticism made by the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Whittaker) in his comments on the suggestions put forward by the hon. member from Kam-loops-Cariboo (Mr. Marchand). The farmer would get $100
per animal, not $38 as stated by the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary.
It is extremely important that the provinces act with the federal government to work out, as soon as possible, a uniform policy for the whole country. This is not being done at present. Alberta and Saskatchewan have moved to improve the cash flow to farmers hit by low cow prices by paying cash advances of $75 per head. Manitoba has made cash advances available to farmers who wish to feed their own Stocker calves. Ontario has provided low interest loans to producers of feeder calves. Quebec has made outright grants to help farmers winter their animals. New Brunswick will pay farmers up to $5,000 over the next three years to help them increase the size of their herds. All this has been done without consulting the federal Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan).
It is important that there be a truly national plan to ensure that the beef industry survives and that the consumer gets top quality meat at a fair price. These two things are more closely interrelated than most people realize, because if the beef industry falters in the face of unrealistically low prices the result will be abnormally high prices for consumers in the future.
